title: Goldman Sachs Bans Staff From Betting on Elections and Markets on Prediction Platforms
excerpt: Wall Street banks restrict employee trading on Kalshi and Polymarket amid insider trading cases, allowing bets only on sports and entertainment.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Goldman Sachs prohibits employee trading on prediction markets for financial and political events.
  • Repeated violations may lead to termination or profit forfeiture over $200.
  • Other banks like JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley have similar restrictions amid insider trading concerns.
  • Recent insider trading cases prompted stricter rules for Wall Street employees.
  • Prediction market platforms face regulatory scrutiny and potential bans in several countries.
Wall Street's Prediction Market Crackdown
›Goldman Sachs bans trading on Kalshi and Polymarket for financial events.
›JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley have enacted similar restrictions.
›Hedge funds Point72 and Balyasny ban all personal prediction market trading.
›Violations may lead to profit forfeiture or termination.
  • Goldman Sachs has banned employees from trading on prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket for contracts tied to financial markets, elections, and geopolitical events.
  • Repeated violations can result in termination; employees may be forced to forfeit profits over $200 or donate them to charity.
  • JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, and hedge funds Point72 and Balyasny have enacted similar restrictions amid rising insider trading concerns.
  • The crackdown follows a Google engineer’s $1.2 million Polymarket profit using insider information and a soldier’s $400,000 bet on the Venezuela regime change.

Goldman Sachs has barred its employees from placing bets on prediction market platforms related to financial markets, political elections, and geopolitical events, according to an internal policy update first reported by Bloomberg News.

The new rules prohibit trading on event contracts tied to specific companies — including Goldman Sachs itself — as well as election outcomes, macroeconomic data, and ceasefire timelines in active conflicts. Staff may still bet on sports and entertainment contracts.

Harsh Penalties for Violations

The bank warned that employees who violate the policy repeatedly could face dismissal or have their trading accounts closed. In cases of improper trades, Goldman reserves the right to claw back profits exceeding $200 or direct the gains to charity, according to a document seen by Bloomberg.

“Trading using material non-public information is prohibited in all markets where Goldman Sachs operates.”

— Goldman Sachs spokesperson

The restriction is notable given that Goldman CEO David Solomon publicly called prediction market platforms “very interesting” in January and said he had met with heads of two leading platforms. Six months later, his bank shut the door on employee participation.

Wall Street’s Broader Crackdown

Goldman is not alone. Reuters reported that multiple major Wall Street banks have added prediction market rules to their employee codes of conduct. Morgan Stanley has incorporated clauses into its code of conduct, while Bank of America restricts employees from trading company-specific, macroeconomic, and financial services event contracts.

JPMorgan Chase has advised employees to “act cautiously” without issuing a formal ban. Hedge funds Point72 Asset Management and Balyasny Asset Management have gone further, banning all personal prediction market trading with no category exemptions.

A String of Insider Trading Cases

The restrictions follow several high-profile cases that raised alarms about nonpublic information flowing into prediction markets. In May, the Justice Department and the Commodities Futures Trading Commission charged Google software engineer Michele Spagnuolo with profiting $1.2 million on Polymarket after accessing confidential information at work.

In January, a U.S. soldier allegedly made more than $400,000 betting on the removal of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, who was ousted and captured by American forces. Wisconsin Representative Bryan Steil introduced legislation in June to prevent certain public officials from wagering on policy outcomes, though the bill did not name specific officials.

Regulatory Reckoning

Prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket have grown rapidly, offering contracts on events from elections to weather. But their expansion has triggered regulatory scrutiny. Several U.S. states have sued both platforms for allegedly running illegal gambling operations, and countries including Canada, Australia, Switzerland, and France have banned them outright.

Polymarket is now seeking regulatory approval to offer margin trading for U.S. users, a move likely to intensify the debate over whether these platforms represent financial innovation or gambling in fintech clothing.
